speakers: Todd Sohn (chief chartist and ETF strategist, Strategas)
summary: June 2026 chart review: Sohn reads stock and ETF charts using RSI, 200-day slopes and ETF flow data. Main message: tech/semis dominate the S&P, flows are one-sided, leveraged and thematic ETFs signal froth, and index/factor ETFs are not diversified.

coverage.note: chartist philosophy, RSI, semis 18% of S&P
semis dominance, software, GEV, Amazon charts
Meta, Oracle, Microsoft, 200-day slope, chart review habit
Google, ETF share of volume, leveraged ETFs boom
beta factor extremes, sector hedges, mutual fund vs ETF flows
active outflows, S&P concentration, diversification illusion
sector ETF flows since March 30, factor overlap, leveraged ETF usage
thematic ETF drawdowns and Sharpe, groups above 15% weight, flow percentile
cyclical vs defensive flows, financials, healthcare, small caps
energy flows, discretionary equal weight, staples decline
REITs, quality ETF, money market funds, gold
gold and Bitcoin ETF outflows, closing lessons

claims.speaker: Todd Sohn
claims.quote: something reaching a new high without being as overbought, that can be a little bit of a warning sign. Or something making a new low without being as oversold, that can be a a perhaps change of trend
claims.claim: RSI divergence is a guideline: a price making a new high with weaker RSI warns of a trend change, and a new low with less oversold RSI suggests selling pressure is easing.
claims.direction: reduce on bearish divergence; look for bottom on bullish divergence

claims.speaker: Todd Sohn
claims.quote: They're 18% of the S&P 500 now, going on 19%. And where were they 10 years ago? 2%.
claims.claim: Semiconductors have risen from about 2% to 18-19% of the S&P 500 in ten years after a massive run since the 30 March 2026 low, so the index is dominated by one group.

claims.speaker: Todd Sohn
claims.quote: if something happened and this index I'll just going to make this up collapsed. Right. By definition the market would collapse.
claims.claim: Because semis are 18-19% of the cap-weighted index, a collapse in semis would pull index-based investors down regardless of internal rotation.
claims.conditions: Index investors feel it on the surface

claims.speaker: Todd Sohn
claims.quote: in the technical world they have what I would describe as mean reverted back to some moving averages, you know, your 200 day, your 50 day.
claims.claim: Software stocks rebounded to their 50/200-day moving averages from oversold levels, which signals a reprieve, not a buy; speculate only with defined risk (stop levels or options).
claims.direction: no outright long; use options with limited premium risk
claims.conditions: After a bad year and oversold sentiment
claims.testable: partly - moving-average reversion rules are testable

claims.speaker: Todd Sohn
claims.quote: If you showed me this ticker, this chart without any without telling me what the ticker was, I would tell you it's going to be a buy pretty soon, right? You have a great trend, you got very overbought.
claims.claim: A strong uptrend that became overbought then consolidates while profit-taking (GEV) is a buyable pullback set-up.
claims.indicator: price trend with RSI overbought then consolidation
claims.direction: long on consolidation in an uptrend

claims.speaker: Todd Sohn
claims.quote: we really like to work off of the slopes of moving averages. Everyone uses a 200-day moving average.
claims.claim: The slope of the 200-day moving average gauges trend: rising means the trend is up, while a flat or rolling-over slope on a stock when the market makes new highs signals a deteriorating trend (Meta, Oracle).
claims.direction: avoid/short names whose 200-day slope turns flat or down while the index makes new highs
claims.conditions: Especially when the index, equal-weight and small caps are at new highs

claims.speaker: Todd Sohn
claims.quote: One, you have a market that is making a new high. S&P 500, equal S&P 500, small caps are making new highs. This is not made a new high in months.
claims.claim: A stock failing to make a new high for months while the S&P, equal-weight S&P and small caps are at highs is a relative-weakness warning (Meta).
claims.direction: short or avoid laggards in a rising market
claims.testable: yes - relative new-high filter is testable

claims.speaker: Todd Sohn
claims.quote: print out 100 stock charts. S&P 100.
claims.claim: A qualitative cross-sectional review of 100 large-cap charts quickly reveals market breadth and which stocks are leading or lagging.

claims.speaker: Todd Sohn
claims.quote: you're already almost retesting the lows from earlier in the year, what in the spring, in April. Right. Which to me, that's a little bit of a red flag.
claims.claim: A stock retesting its spring lows while the market makes new highs (Microsoft) is a red flag of relative weakness.
claims.indicator: stock retest of prior lows vs index highs

claims.speaker: Todd Sohn
claims.quote: On an average day, ETFs will do about 30% of volume.
claims.claim: ETFs account for about 30% of US exchange volume on an average day and rise to 40-45% in stressful periods as investors adjust exposure, so ETF volume share is a stress gauge.
claims.indicator: ETF share of US exchange volume
claims.testable: yes - volume share series is observable

claims.speaker: Todd Sohn
claims.quote: $200 billion category. Leveraged ETFs. Up massively since 2020.
claims.claim: Leveraged ETFs are a roughly 200bn category up massively since 2020, with a new wave of 2x single-stock and theme products launching.

claims.speaker: Todd Sohn
claims.quote: Now remember it's only on a daily basis. This is not From point to point it doesn't necessarily do that.
claims.claim: Leveraged ETFs reset daily, so multi-day returns slip from the stated multiple and fees accumulate; they are trading vehicles, not buy-and-hold.

claims.speaker: Todd Sohn
claims.quote: Google has the best chart.
claims.claim: Among big tech charts, Alphabet is strongest after a very extended, overbought run and is similar to GEV; Meta and Microsoft look weak.
claims.indicator: price chart strength relative to peers
claims.direction: long Google/GEV; short or avoid Meta/Microsoft
claims.testable: partly - rule-based chart ranking is testable

claims.speaker: Todd Sohn
claims.quote: the performance of say semis versus staples has gotten to historically extreme territory.
claims.claim: The one-year return of high-beta versus low-beta (and low-vol) stocks is at historical extremes, which argues for awareness of mean reversion though it is still a bull market.
claims.indicator: rolling 1-year beta factor spread (top vs bottom decile)
claims.direction: eventual mean reversion in low vol vs high beta
claims.conditions: Still a bull market; not a sell signal

claims.speaker: Todd Sohn
claims.quote: But if you're looking for stuff to hedge tech, look in healthcare, discretionary, financial
claims.claim: Hedges for tech concentration should come from lagging sectors: healthcare, discretionary and financials on rolling six-month relative performance.

claims.speaker: Todd Sohn
claims.quote: mutual fund flows on a cumulative basis are now negative since 1984.
claims.claim: Cumulative mutual-fund flows since 1984 are negative (about -5.1tn, all from active equity funds) while ETFs absorb the flows, so assets in mutual funds depend on market gains.
claims.indicator: cumulative ETF vs mutual fund flows

claims.speaker: Todd Sohn
claims.quote: most of those outflows are coming from actively managed mutual funds
claims.claim: Money is rotating from active mutual funds to cheaper, transparent ETFs including active ETFs.
claims.indicator: active mutual fund outflows; active ETF inflows

claims.speaker: Todd Sohn
claims.quote: So, if I own the S&P 500, if I own Russell 1000 Growth, if I own a thematic fund, I have a lot of Nvidia, Microsoft, Meta exposure.
claims.claim: Cap-weighted index, growth and thematic funds all hold the same mega-cap tech names, so index ownership is not diversification (tech near 38-40% of the S&P) and a day of unwind hurts.

claims.speaker: Todd Sohn
claims.quote: the amount of money tracking the S&P is far far far larger than Italian stocks.
claims.claim: International diversification is not a fix because the US index is so large that single-country caps (Korea, Italy) are small compared with S&P-tracking money.

claims.speaker: Todd Sohn
claims.quote: 27 billion into tech ETFs, give or take, since the March 30th low.
claims.claim: Cumulative sector ETF flows since the 30 March low show about +27bn into tech and -4.4bn into all other sectors combined, concentrated in semis and hardware, so flows are one-sided and vulnerable to an unwind.

claims.speaker: Todd Sohn
claims.quote: Let's say, "Okay, I'm going to buy the quality factor ETF."
claims.claim: Quality and momentum factor ETFs now mirror the S&P (R-squared near 1) because the S&P has morphed into a quality index loaded with tech, so factor ETFs no longer diversify.
claims.direction: drop quality ETF; buy S&P instead
claims.conditions: Valid when top index names dominate quality and momentum screens

claims.speaker: Todd Sohn
claims.quote: 200 billion in assets across a few hundred products now.
claims.claim: Leveraged ETF usage is at a record, with 2x/3x products profitable at about 1% fees and retail-friendly (no margin), signalling froth.

claims.speaker: Todd Sohn
claims.quote: because these funds rebalance at the end of every day to reset that to a daily exposure, it's adding more volatility into the market.
claims.claim: Daily-rebalanced leveraged ETFs buy into rallies (and sell into drops) at the close, amplifying volatility on big move days.
claims.conditions: Larger when leveraged single-stock AUM is high

claims.speaker: Todd Sohn
claims.quote: These didn't exist until 2022.
claims.claim: Leveraged single-stock ETFs (hundreds, on ever smaller caps such as quantum and space names, popular with retail) are a new game since 2022 and a froth indicator.
claims.indicator: count and AUM of leveraged single-stock ETFs

claims.speaker: Todd Sohn
claims.quote: It's reflective of herding behavior.
claims.claim: Heavy inflows into a hot theme ETF reflect performance chasing and herding rather than diversification.

claims.speaker: Todd Sohn
claims.quote: the average 3-year drawdown is is 32%.
claims.claim: Thematic ETFs have an average 3-year drawdown of 32% (cannabis about 80%) and 70% have a Sharpe ratio below 1, so chasing single themes is poor on risk-adjusted terms.
claims.indicator: thematic ETF 3-year drawdown and Sharpe ratio
claims.testable: yes - thematic ETF universe stats computable

claims.speaker: Todd Sohn
claims.quote: has there any been any other groups above 15% in the S&P?
claims.claim: Since 1990 only tech hardware (to about 30% in the bubble), energy (mid-2000s) and software (late 2010s) exceeded 15% index weight; two of three ended badly for the market and the group, a roadmap for how far concentration can run.
claims.conditions: Small sample of three; the 2018 case was a GICS reclassification

claims.speaker: Todd Sohn
claims.quote: Flows are just a it's a temperature barometer. They're not necessarily a signal.
claims.claim: Equity ETF flows ranked as a one-year percentile are a sentiment gauge; broad flows are lukewarm, so there is no sign of a broad market top even though tech is extreme.
claims.indicator: percentile of equity ETF flows over trailing 1 year
claims.testable: yes - percentile series easy to build

claims.speaker: Todd Sohn
claims.quote: Just a measure of risk risk appetite.
claims.claim: Cyclical (ex-tech) ETF flows minus defensive flows measure risk appetite, and it is subdued, with money going only to tech and power-related industrials.
claims.indicator: cyclical minus defensive sector ETF flows

claims.speaker: Todd Sohn
claims.quote: I kind of look at that as bullish, to be honest, but I think it has a lot to do with the private credit headlines.
claims.claim: No flows into financials amid private-credit worries; Sohn reads the unease as contrarian-bullish.

claims.speaker: Todd Sohn
claims.quote: It's health care shrunk shrunk from 16% of the S&P to 8%.
claims.claim: Health care fell from 16% to 8% of the S&P after years of outflows, so extreme underperformance sets up a possible reversion to the mean (low conviction after a year of being early).
claims.conditions: Speaker says timing has been wrong for a year

claims.speaker: Todd Sohn
claims.quote: last year small cap ETFs had outflows. That was the first time since 2011.
claims.claim: Small-cap ETF outflows in 2025 were the first since 2011 and flows have only partly returned, showing weak endorsement of small caps.

claims.speaker: Todd Sohn
claims.quote: There was a massive sugar rush to energy from uh it was a February 27th.
claims.claim: Energy ETF flows spiked after the 27 Feb war move and then fell as oil collapsed on the 14 June deal announcement, so flow surges into a theme often mark the profit-taking phase.

claims.speaker: Todd Sohn
claims.quote: cap weight discretionary is skewed by Amazon and Tesla.
claims.claim: Cap-weighted consumer discretionary is dominated by Amazon and Tesla, so equal-weight discretionary (in the bottom decile) is the better gauge of the consumer and of K-shaped weakness; test sector ideas on equal weight.

claims.speaker: Todd Sohn
claims.quote: It will take a market freak out for algorithms to buy consumer staples again, I think, is what is happening.
claims.claim: Staples fell from about 19% to 4.5% of the S&P and now lose allocation to covered-call, buffered and income ETFs, so they only attract flows in a market shock.
claims.conditions: Algorithmic buying of defensives only after a shock

claims.speaker: Todd Sohn
claims.quote: in the tech the 2000s extreme. Way too extreme right now. But if you ever had to have another 2000 environment, the REITs actually went up during it.
claims.claim: REITs diversified during the 2000 tech-bubble unwind and rose, so they are a potential diversifier if tech concentration unwinds.
claims.direction: long REITs as a tech-bubble hedge

claims.speaker: Todd Sohn
claims.quote: it's the R squared of this ETF, which is about a $50 ETF, is near perfect to the S&P 500.
claims.claim: A quality ETF that has near-perfect R-squared to the S&P adds nothing; buy the index or a truly different exposure.
claims.indicator: R-squared of quality ETF vs S&P 500

claims.speaker: Todd Sohn
claims.quote: there's 8 trillion of money market funds and as a percentage of the bond agg, that's very elevated. It's about 25%.
claims.claim: Money-market funds (8tn, about 25% of the bond aggregate) are taking share from bond managers and are dry powder if the rate regime changes.
claims.indicator: money-market fund assets as % of the bond aggregate

claims.speaker: Todd Sohn
claims.quote: Chris always likes to say pay attention when stuff that is supposed to behave one way does not.
claims.claim: Gold falling despite war and inflation fears (a blow-off after metal mania, higher rates and a firmer dollar) is a case where an asset not acting as expected deserves attention.

claims.speaker: Todd Sohn
claims.quote: I've seen a lot of money coming out coming out of gold ETFs. So, that kind of perks my interest of well, maybe this thing will start to bottom out.
claims.claim: Heavy outflows from gold and Bitcoin ETFs signal capitulation and a low bar, so contrarian bottoming is possible (Bitcoin interest shifted to prediction markets).

claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.quote: if you own an index and you think therefore you're diversified, you're actually no longer diversified because tech so dominates.
claims.claim: Tech is near 40% of the S&P and over 50% with Alphabet and Amazon; with flows one-sided, an unwind would have no place to hide.
claims.indicator: tech and mega-cap weight in S&P 500
